name: modular-monolith
context: Single deployable unit organized into loosely coupled, domain-oriented modules with clear boundaries while retaining operational simplicity
benefits: Team autonomy: Teams own modules independently without stepping on each other
Clear boundaries: Domain-driven module decomposition reduces coupling between bounded contexts
Operational simplicity: Single deployment, single database, simpler operations than microservices
Independent development: Modules can be developed by separate teams with minimal coordination
Evolution path: Modules that need independence can be extracted to services later
Testability: Modules can be tested in isolation with mocked dependencies
Refactoring safety: Clear module boundaries make large-scale refactoring safer
Improved performance: In-process communication eliminates network latency overhead
Easier transaction management: Modules can share the same database
Lower operational complexity: Reduced overhead compared to distributed microservices
tradeoffs: Module discipline required: Developers must respect boundaries; refactoring needed when boundaries blur
Shared kernel maintenance: Keeping shared kernel small and stable requires governance
Deployment coupling: All modules deployed together; one module's bug affects all
Database schema coordination: Schema changes affecting multiple modules require coordination
Scaling limitations: Scales as a single unit; cannot scale individual modules independently
Boundary erosion risk: Without enforcement tools, modular monoliths can degrade into traditional monoliths
use_cases: Team size is 5-50 with domain-aligned ownership and clear module boundaries
Needing domain-driven boundaries without microservices operational overhead
Planning eventual extraction of modules to services (migration path)
Domain has clear bounded contexts that map to business capabilities
Needing operational simplicity while maintaining modularity
Starting a new project where domain boundaries are well-understood
Improving an existing monolith with clear module boundaries
Requiring faster development velocity without distributed complexity
avoid_when: Small teams with simple requirements that don't warrant modularization overhead
Independent scaling of specific modules is a primary requirement
Very high transaction throughput requirements that demand per-module scaling
Strict isolation between teams with different deployment cadences is required
Team prefers pure microservices approach with mature DevOps maturity
Domain boundaries are not yet clear and exploration is needed
component_types: Domain Module: Self-contained module with domain logic, entities, services, repositories, and events
Shared Kernel: Minimal common types, interfaces, and utilities shared across modules
Module Facade: Stable public API that encapsulates module implementation details
Module Registry: Central registry for module discovery and service resolution
Event Bus: In-process event publication/subscription for asynchronous module communication
Plugin Interface: Abstract interface (IPlugin) for hot-swappable extensions
Plugin Registry: Discovery, loading, and management of runtime-extensible plugins
technology_stack: Java, Kotlin, Ruby, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, C#/.NET
PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle (shared schema per module)
anti_patterns: Shared database access: Modules directly modifying another module's data instead of going through APIs
Leaky abstractions: Exposing internal implementation details through public API
Premature extraction: Extracting services before clear operational need (leading to distributed monolith)
Insufficient module isolation: Too-tight coupling that defeats the purpose of modularity
Cross-module joins: Database queries spanning multiple module data stores
Big ball of mud: Modular structure that degrades into entangled monolith over time
Chatty modules: Modules that are too interdependent, indicating incorrect boundaries
design_principles: Domain Module Isolation: Each module encapsulates its own domain logic, entities, and services. Independent module directories with clear ownership ensure that changes to one domain don't ripple through others.
Explicit Module Dependencies: Dependencies between modules are explicit and controlled through the shared kernel pattern and module API contracts. No hidden dependencies allowed.
Data Ownership: Each module owns its data; no direct cross-module database access. Module-scoped repositories and module databases enforce this boundary.
Public API Contracts: Modules expose stable facades; implementation details are hidden. The facade pattern and module API interfaces ensure clean separation.
Single Deployable Unit: All modules deployed together as one artifact. Monolithic build with a single deployment pipeline ensures atomic updates.
Event-Driven Communication: Modules communicate through domain events rather than direct dependencies, enabling loose coupling and independent evolution.
Enforced Boundaries: Use tooling (ArchUnit, Spring Modulith) to enforce module boundaries. Automated checks prevent boundary erosion.
